analysis.one_liner: Caps US global warming pollution with a trading program and cuts emissions 65% by 2050.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late September 2006 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never received a hearing or vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to set binding national limits on carbon dioxide and other heat-trapping gases, starting with 1.5% cuts per year through 2019 and reaching a 65% reduction below 2000 levels by 2050. It creates a cap-and-trade market for emission allowances, with auction proceeds going into a Climate Reinvestment Fund and a ban on giving polluters free allowances that produce windfall profits. It also requires passenger-vehicle emission standards at least as strict as California's, forces electric utilities to hit energy-savings and renewable-power targets, requires large oil companies to install ethanol (E-85) pumps, doubles tax credits for efficient vehicles, and directs the SEC to make large companies disclose their climate-related financial risks.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans exposed to climate damage — heat waves, droughts, wildfires, coastal flooding — plus consumers who would save money through mandated energy-efficiency programs, buyers of advanced-technology vehicles who would get larger tax credits, and workers in carbon-heavy regions, for whom the bill directs transition assistance. Investors would get standardized disclosure of climate risks from large companies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, and communities exposed to climate damage

how_it_helps.text: Sets mandatory economy-wide emission targets — at least 1.5% reductions each year 2010–2019, 2.5% each year 2020–2029, and 3.5% each year 2030–2050, aiming for a 65% cut below 2000 levels by 2050 [S3].

Requires the allowance plan to prohibit any free distribution of allowances that would create windfall profits for covered polluters, and deposits auction proceeds and penalties into a Climate Reinvestment Fund for emission-reduction projects and help for affected workers and regions [S3].

Requires retail electricity suppliers to cut customer electricity use and peak demand — reaching a 9% cumulative reduction in electricity use by 2020 — backed by a fee of at least 4 cents per kilowatt-hour for suppliers that miss the targets, a program the bill's findings say would save consumers money [S3].

Requires passenger-vehicle emission standards at least as strict as California's 2004 rules, with revisions every five years, and doubles or creates federal tax credits for fuel-cell, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and advanced-technology vehicle purchases and manufacturing [S3].

Requires retail electricity suppliers to source 20% of their power from renewables by 2020, and obliges major oil companies to install E-85 ethanol pumps at up to half their owned and branded stations [S3].
Directs the SEC to require companies with over $1 billion in market value to disclose to investors their emissions exposure and the economic risks global warming poses to them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered polluters — power plants, refineries, and other major stationary sources — would pay for emission allowances or penalties and annual reporting costs. Electric utilities that miss efficiency or renewable targets would pay fees, with costs potentially passed to customers. Major oil companies would bear the full cost of installing E-85 pumps. The Treasury would forgo revenue from the expanded vehicle tax credits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel emitters, utilities, and oil companies

drawbacks.text: Cap-and-trade compliance costs on power plants and fuel producers could raise energy prices; the bill itself declares a goal of mitigating energy cost increases to consumers, particularly low-income consumers, acknowledging this risk [S3].

The renewable fuel mandate rises to at least 60 billion gallons by 2030 and utilities pay at least 4 cents per kilowatt-hour for missing efficiency targets — costs that would largely flow into gasoline and electricity prices, with effects on food and fuel costs from large-scale ethanol use not addressed in the bill [S3].

Doubling vehicle purchase credits and creating a new 35% manufacturing credit reduces federal revenue, and the manufacturing credit's design depends on manufacturers' tax capacity rather than direct per-vehicle payments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's central promise — a legally binding, decades-long emissions path with anti-windfall rules for polluters — is aimed squarely at public benefits, and it includes consumer-cost protections, transition aid for affected workers, and direct consumer credits. Its real costs are higher energy prices passed through from polluters and utilities, revenue lost to vehicle tax credits, and the risk that large ethanol mandates create their own price problems. The design details (how much to auction versus allocate, how credit trading works) would have been settled by later regulation, so the ultimate burden on households depended on implementation.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the 109th Congress ended, never receiving a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator John Kerry introduced the bill on September 29, 2006, for himself and Senator Olympia Snowe, making it one of the few climate bills of that Congress with a Republican cosponsor [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day — its only action [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major emitters — coal-fired power, refineries, and other large fossil fuel users — continued operating without emission caps or allowance costs, and no one received the bill's consumer credits, efficiency savings, or climate protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large emitters, who avoided new pollution caps

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, proposing economy-wide emission caps, vehicle standards, utility mandates, and vehicle tax credits.

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress expired.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — but the Republican-controlled Senate never acted on the bill, so no vote reveals where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power and other large fossil fuel emitters
industries.note: They would face a binding emissions cap, allowance auctions with no free allowances creating windfalls, civil penalties at twice the allowance price for excess emissions, and annual public reporting of emissions.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and retail electricity suppliers
industries.note: They face a 20% renewable-power mandate by 2020 and escalating energy-savings targets with a 4-cents-per-kilowatt-hour fee for shortfalls, but also gain a tradable credit market and demand for renewables they can sell.
Companies with 4,500 or more stations must install E-85 ethanol pumps at up to half their outlets at their own expense, but they can earn and sell credits for exceeding the requirement.

The bill replaces the existing renewable-fuel schedule with rising mandates — 10 billion gallons by 2010, 30 billion by 2020, 60 billion by 2030 — guaranteeing a market and forcing oil companies to build the retail infrastructure to sell their product.

They face passenger-vehicle emission standards at least as strict as California's, but receive doubled consumer purchase credits that expand their advanced-technology market and a new credit worth 35% of qualified investment in advanced-vehicle manufacturing facilities.
A national renewable portfolio standard rising to 20% of electricity sales creates a guaranteed, credit-tracked market for wind, solar, and other renewable generation.
